entries.f0945be3331c7420ea2b1cab78d3f1aad7f3ab15: <div sID="gen12581" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="116" osisID="Ps.116" sID="Ps.116"/> <div eID="gen12581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12582" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12583" type="x-p"/> This is a thanksgiving psalm; it is not certain whether David penned it upon any particular occasion or upon a general review of the many gracious deliverances God had wrought for him, out of six troubles and seven, which deliverances draw from him many very lively expressions of devotion, love, and gratitude; and with similar pious affections our souls should be lifted up to God in singing it. Observe, I. The great distress and danger that the psalmist was in, which almost drove him to despair, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.3">ver. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.10">10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.11">11</reference>. II. The application he made to God in that distress, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.4">ver. 4</reference>. III. The experience he had of God's goodness to him, in answer to prayer; God heard him (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.1-Ps.116.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>), pitied him (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.5-Ps.116.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>), delivered him, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.8">ver. 8</reference>. IV His care respecting the acknowledgments he should make of the goodness of God to him, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.12">ver. 12</reference>. 1. He will love God, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.1">ver. 1</reference>. 2. He will continue to call upon him, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.2">ver. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.13">13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.17">17</reference>. 3. He will rest in him, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.7">ver. 7</reference>. 4. He will walk before him, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.9">ver. 9</reference>. 5. He will pay his vows of thanksgiving, in which he will own the tender regard God had to him, and this publicly, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.13-Ps.116.15">ver. 13-15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.17-Ps.116.19">17-19</reference>. Lastly, He will continue God's faithful servant to his life's end, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">ver. 16</reference>. These are such breathings of a holy soul as bespeak it very happy.
entries.6b9c1285121f33eb8882187d0118823e16fb2ec1: <div eID="gen12583" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12582" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Grateful Acknowledgments.</title> <div sID="gen12584" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I love the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , because he hath heard my voice <hi type="italic">and</hi> my supplications. <hi type="super">2</hi> Because he hath inclined his ear unto me, therefore will I call upon <hi type="italic">him</hi> as long as I live. <hi type="super">3</hi> The sorrows of death compassed me, and the pains of hell gat hold upon me: I found trouble and sorrow. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then called I upon the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , I beseech thee, deliver my soul. <hi type="super">5</hi> Gracious <hi type="italic">is</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and righteous; yea, our God <hi type="italic">is</hi> merciful. <hi type="super">6</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> preserveth the simple: I was brought low, and he helped me. <hi type="super">7</hi> Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath dealt bountifully with thee. <hi type="super">8</hi> For thou hast delivered my soul from death, mine eyes from tears, <hi type="italic">and</hi> my feet from falling. <hi type="super">9</hi> I will walk before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the land of the living. <div eID="gen12584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12585" type="x-p"/> In this part of the psalm we have, <div eID="gen12585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12586" type="x-p"/> I. A general account of David's experience, and his pious resolutions (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.1-Ps.116.2">v. 1, 2</reference>), which are as the contents of the whole psalm, and give an idea of it. 1. He had experienced God's goodness to him in answer to prayer: <hi type="italic">He has heard my voice and my supplications.</hi> David, in straits, had humbly and earnestly begged mercy of God, and God had heard him, that is, had graciously accepted his prayer, taken cognizance of his case, and granted him an answer of peace. <hi type="italic">He has inclined his ear to me.</hi> This intimates his readiness and willingness to hear prayer; he lays his ear, as it were, to the mouth of prayer, to hear it, though it be but whispered <hi type="italic">in groanings that cannot be uttered.</hi> He <hi type="italic">hearkens and hears,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.8.6">Jer. viii. 6</reference>. Yet it implies, also, that it is wonderful condescension in God to hear prayer; it is bowing his ear. Lord, what is man, that God should thus stoop to him!—2. He resolved, in consideration thereof, to devote himself entirely to God and to his honour. (1.) He will love God the better. He begins the psalm somewhat abruptly with a profession of that which his heart was full of: <hi type="italic">I love the Lord</hi> (as <reference osisRef="Ps.18.1">Ps. xviii. 1</reference>); and fitly does he begin with this, in compliance with the first and great commandment and with God's end in all the gifts of his bounty to us. "I love him only, and nothing besides him, but what I love for him." God's love of compassion towards us justly requires our love of complacency in him. (2.) He will love prayer the better: <hi type="italic">Therefore I will call upon him.</hi> The experiences we have had of God's goodness to us, in answer to prayer, are great encouragements to us to continue praying; we have sped well, notwithstanding our unworthiness and our infirmities in prayer, and therefore why may we not? God answers prayer, to make us love it, and expects this from us, in return for his favour. Why should we glean in any other field when we have been so well treated in this? Nay, <hi type="italic">I will call upon him as long as I live</hi> (Heb., <hi type="italic">In my days</hi>), every day, to the last day. Note, As long as we continue living we must continue praying. This breath we must breathe till we breathe our last, because then we shall take our leave of it, and till then we have continual occasion for it. <div eID="gen12586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12587" type="x-p"/> II. A more particular narrative of God's gracious dealings with him and the good impressions thereby made upon him. <div eID="gen12587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12588" type="x-p"/> 1. God, in his dealings with him, showed himself a good God, and therefore he bears this testimony to him, and leaves it upon record (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Gracious is the Lord, and righteous.</hi> He is righteous, and did me no wrong in afflicting me; he is gracious, and was very kind in supporting and delivering me." Let us all speak of God as we have found; and have we ever found him otherwise than just and good? No; <hi type="italic">our God is merciful,</hi> merciful to us, and <hi type="italic">it is of his mercies that we are not consumed.</hi> <div eID="gen12588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12589" type="x-p"/> (1.) Let us review David's experiences. [1.] He was in great distress and trouble (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">The sorrows of death compassed me,</hi> that is, such sorrows as were likely to be his death, such as were thought to be the very pangs of death. Perhaps the extremity of bodily pain, or trouble of mind, is called here <hi type="italic">the pains of hell,</hi> terror of conscience arising from sense of guilt. Note, The sorrows of death are great sorrows, and the pains of hell great pains. Let us <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> give diligence to prepare for the former, that we may escape the latter. These <hi type="italic">compassed</hi> him on every side; they arrested him, <hi type="italic">got hold upon him,</hi> so that he could not escape. <hi type="italic">Without were fightings, within were fears. "I found trouble and sorrow;</hi> not only they found me, but I found them." Those that are melancholy have a great deal of sorrow of their own finding, a great deal of trouble which they create to themselves, by indulging fancy and passion; this has sometimes been the infirmity of good men. When God's providence makes our condition bad let us not by our own imprudence make it worse. [2.] In his trouble he had recourse to God by faithful and fervent prayer, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.4">v. 4</reference>. He tells us that he prayed: <hi type="italic">Then called I upon the name of the Lord;</hi> then, when he was brought to the last extremity, then he made use of this, not as the last remedy, but as the old and only remedy, which he had found a salve for every sore. He tells us what his prayer was; it was short, but to the purpose: "<hi type="italic">O Lord! I beseech thee, deliver my soul;</hi> save me from death, and save me from sin, for that is it that is killing to the soul." Both the humility and the fervency of his prayer are intimated in these words, <hi type="italic">O Lord! I beseech thee.</hi> When we come to the throne of grace we must come as beggars for an alms, for necessary food. The following words (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.5">v. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">Gracious is the Lord,</hi> may be taken as part of his prayer, as a plea to enforce his request and encourage his faith and hope: "Lord <hi type="italic">deliver my soul,</hi> for thou art <hi type="italic">gracious</hi> and <hi type="italic">merciful,</hi> and that only I depend upon for relief." [3.] God, in answer to his prayer, came in with seasonable and effectual relief. He found by experience that God is gracious and merciful, and in his compassion <hi type="italic">preserves the simple,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.116.6">v. 6</reference>. Because they are simple (that is, sincere, and upright, and without guile) therefore God preserves them, as he preserved Paul, who had his conversation in the world <hi type="italic">not with fleshly wisdom, but in simplicity and godly sincerity.</hi> Though they are simple (that is, weak, and helpless, and unable to shift for themselves, men of no depth, no design) yet God preserves them, because they commit themselves to him and have no confidence in their own sufficiency. Those who by faith put themselves under God's protection shall be safe. <div eID="gen12589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12590" type="x-p"/> (2.) Let David speak his own experience. [1.] God supported him under his troubles: "<hi type="italic">I was brought low,</hi> was plunged into the depth of misery, and then <hi type="italic">he helped me,</hi> helped me both to bear the worst and to hope the best, helped me to pray, else desire had failed, helped me to wait, else faith had failed. I was one of the simple ones whom God preserved, the poor man who <hi type="italic">cried and the Lord heard him,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.34.6">Ps. xxxiv. 6</reference>. Note, God's people are never brought so low but that everlasting arms are under them, and those cannot sink who are thus sustained. Nay, it is in the time of need, at the dead lift, that God chooses to help, <reference osisRef="Deut.32.36">Deut. xxxii. 36</reference>. [2.] God saved him out of his troubles (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast delivered,</hi> which means either the preventing of the distress he was ready to fall into or the recovering of him from the distress he was already in. God graciously delivered, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> His <hi type="italic">soul from death.</hi> Note, It is God's great mercy to us that we are alive; and the mercy is the more sensible if we have been at death's door and yet have been spared and raised up, just turned to destruction and yet ordered to return. That a life so often forfeited, and so often exposed, should yet be lengthened out, is a miracle of mercy. The deliverance of the soul from spiritual and eternal death is especially to be acknowledged by all those who are now sanctified and shall be shortly glorified. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> His <hi type="italic">eyes from tears,</hi> that is, his heart from inordinate grief. It is a great mercy to be kept either from the occasions of sorrow, the evil that causes grief, or, at least, from being swallowed up with over-much sorrow. When God comforts those that are cast down, looses the mourners' sackcloth and girds them with gladness, then he delivers <hi type="italic">their eyes from tears,</hi> which yet will not be perfectly done till we come to that world where God shall <hi type="italic">wipe away all tears from our eyes. Thirdly,</hi> His <hi type="italic">feet from falling,</hi> from falling into sin and so into misery. It is a great mercy, when our feet are almost gone, to have God <hi type="italic">hold us by the right hand</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.72.2">Ps. lxxii. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.23">23</reference>), so that though we enter into temptation we are not overcome and overthrown by the temptation. Or, "Thou <hi type="italic">hast delivered my feet from falling</hi> into the grave, when I had one foot there already." <div eID="gen12590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12591" type="x-p"/> 2. David, in his returns of gratitude to God, showed himself a good man. God had done all this for him, and therefore, <div eID="gen12591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12592" type="x-p"/> (1.) He will live a life of delight in God (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Return unto thy rest, O my soul!</hi> [1.] "Repose thyself and be easy, and do not agitate thyself with distrustful disquieting fears as thou hast sometimes done. Quiet thyself, and then enjoy thyself. God has dealt kindly with thee, and therefore thou needest not fear that ever he will deal hardly with thee." [2.] "Repose thyself in God. Return to him as thy rest, and seek not for that rest in the creature which is to be had in him only." God is the soul's rest; in him only it can <hi type="italic">dwell at ease;</hi> to him therefore it must retire, and rejoice in him. He has <hi type="italic">dealt bountifully with us;</hi> he has provided sufficiently for our comfort and refreshment, and encouraged us to come to him for the benefit of it, at all times, upon all occasions; let us therefore be satisfied with that. Return to that rest which Christ gives to <hi type="italic">the weary and heavy-laden,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.11.28">Matt. xi. 28</reference>. Return to thy Noah; his name signifies <hi type="italic">rest,</hi> as the dove, when she found no rest, returned to the ark. I know no word more proper to close our eyes with at night, when we go to sleep, nor to close them with at death, that long sleep, than this, <hi type="italic">Return to thy rest, O my soul!</hi> <div eID="gen12592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12593" type="x-p"/> (2.) He will live a life of devotedness to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will walk before the Lord in the land of the living,</hi> that is, in this world, as long as I continue to live in it. Note, [1.] It is our great duty to <hi type="italic">walk before the Lord,</hi> to do all we do as becomes us in his presence and under his eye, to approve ourselves to him as a holy God by conformity to him as our sovereign Lord, by subjection to his will, and, as a God all-sufficient, by a cheerful confidence in him. <hi type="italic">I am the almighty God; walk before me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.17.1">Gen. xvii. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">We must walk worthy of the Lord unto all well-pleasing.</hi> [2.] The consideration of this, that we are in the land of the living, should engage and quicken us to do so. We are spared and continued in the land of the living by the power, and patience, and tender mercy of our God, and therefore must make conscience of our duty to him. The <hi type="italic">land of the living</hi> is a land of mercy, which we ought to be thankful for; it is a land of opportunity, which we should improve. Canaan is called the <hi type="italic">land of the living</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.26.20">Ezek. xxvi. 20</reference>), and those whose lot is cast in such a valley of vision are in a special manner concerned to <hi type="italic">set the Lord always before them.</hi> If God has delivered our soul from death, we must walk before him. A new life must be a new life indeed.
entries.762941560a88fc09bd8b9f4cc9838f427d31a072: <div eID="gen12593" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Grateful Acknowledgments; Devout Resolutions.</title> <div sID="gen12594" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> I believed, therefore have I spoken: I was greatly afflicted: <hi type="super">11</hi> I said in my haste, All men <hi type="italic">are</hi> liars. <hi type="super">12</hi> What shall I render unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">for</hi> all his benefits toward me? 13 I will take the cup of salvation, and call upon the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">14</hi> I will pay my vows unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> now in the presence of all his people. <hi type="super">15</hi> Precious in the sight of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> the death of his saints. <hi type="super">16</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , truly I <hi type="italic">am</hi> thy servant; I <hi type="italic">am</hi> thy servant, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the son of thine handmaid: thou hast loosed my bonds. <hi type="super">17</hi> I will offer to thee the sacrifice of thanksgiving, and will call upon the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">18</hi> I will pay my vows unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> now in the presence of all his people, <hi type="super">19</hi> In the courts of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> 's house, in the midst of thee, O Jerusalem. Praise ye the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen12594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12595" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint and some other ancient versions make these verses a distinct psalm separate from the former; and some have called it the <hi type="italic">Martyr's psalm,</hi> I suppose for the sake of <reference osisRef="Ps.116.15">v. 15</reference>. Three things David here makes confession of:— <div eID="gen12595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12596" type="x-p"/> I. His faith (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">I believed, therefore have I spoken.</hi> This is quoted by the apostle (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.13">2 Cor. iv. 13</reference>) with application to himself and his fellow-ministers, who, though they suffered for Christ, were not ashamed to own him. David believed the being, providence, and promise of God, particularly the assurance God had given him by Samuel that he should exchange his crook for a sceptre: a great deal of hardship he went through in the belief of this, and therefore he spoke, spoke to God by prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.4">v. 4</reference>), by praise, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.12">v. 12</reference>. Those that believe in God will address themselves to him. He spoke to himself; because he believed, he said to his soul, <hi type="italic">Return to thy rest.</hi> He spoke to others, told his friends what his hope was, and what the ground of it, though it exasperated Saul against him and he was greatly afflicted for it. Note, Those that believe with the heart must confess with the mouth, for the glory of God, the encouragement of others, and to evidence their own sincerity, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.10">Rom. x. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.9.19-Acts.9.20">Acts ix. 19, 20</reference>. Those that live in hope of the kingdom of glory must neither be afraid nor ashamed to own their obligation to him that purchased it for them, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.22">Matt. x. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen12596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12597" type="x-p"/> II. His fear (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">I was greatly afflicted,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">I said in my haste</hi> (somewhat rashly and inconsiderately—in my <hi type="italic">amazement</hi> (so some), when I was in a consternation—<hi type="italic">in my flight</hi> (so others), when Saul was in pursuit of me), <hi type="italic">All men are liars,</hi> all with whom he had to do, Saul and all his courtiers; his friends, who he thought would stand by him, deserted him and disowned him when he fell into disgrace at court. And some think it is especially a reflection on Samuel, who had promised him the kingdom, but deceived him; for, says he, <hi type="italic">I shall one day perish by the hand of Saul,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.27.1">1 Sam. xxvii. 1</reference>. Observe, 1. The faith of the best of saints is not perfect, nor always alike strong and active. David <hi type="italic">believed</hi> and <hi type="italic">spoke well</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.10">v. 10</reference>), but now, through unbelief, he spoke amiss. 2. When we are under great and sore afflictions, especially if they continue long, we are apt to grow weary, to despond, and almost to despair of a good issue. Let us not therefore be harsh in censuring others, but carefully watch over ourselves when we are in trouble, <reference osisRef="Ps.39.1-Ps.39.3">Ps. xxxix. 1-3</reference>. 3. If good men speak amiss, it is in their haste, through the surprise of a temptation, not deliberately and with premeditation, as the wicked man, who <hi type="italic">sits in the seat of the scornful</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Ps. i. 1</reference>), sits and <hi type="italic">speaks against his brother,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.19-Ps.50.20">Ps. l. 19, 20</reference>. 4. What we speak amiss, in haste, we must by repentance unsay again (as David, <reference osisRef="Ps.31.22">Ps. xxxi. 22</reference>), and then it shall not be laid to our charge. Some make this to be no rash word of David's. He was greatly afflicted and forced to fly, but he did not trust in man, nor make flesh his arm. No: he said, "<hi type="italic">All men are liars;</hi> as <hi type="italic">men of low degree are vanity,</hi> so <hi type="italic">men of high degree are a lie,</hi> and therefore my confidence was in God only, and in him I cannot be disappointed." In this sense the apostle seems to take it. <reference osisRef="Rom.3.4">Rom. iii. 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">Let God be true and every man a liar</hi> in comparison with God. All men are fickle and inconstant, and subject to change; and therefore let us cease from man and cleave to God. <div eID="gen12597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12598" type="x-p"/> III. His gratitude, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.12">v. 12</reference>, &c. God had been better to him than his fears, and had graciously delivered him out of his distresses; and, in consideration hereof, <div eID="gen12598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12599" type="x-p"/> 1. He enquires what returns he shall make (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">What shall I render unto the Lord for all his benefits towards me?</hi> Here he speaks, (1.) As one sensible of many mercies received from God—<hi type="italic">all his benefits.</hi> This psalm seems to have been penned upon occasion of some one particular benefit (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.6-Ps.116.7">v. 6, 7</reference>), but in that one he saw many and that one brought many to mind, and therefore now he thinks of all God's benefits towards him. Note, When we speak of God's mercies we should magnify them and speak highly of them. (2.) As one solicitous and studious how to express his gratitude: <hi type="italic">What shall I render unto the Lord?</hi> Not as if he thought he could render any thing proportionable, or as a valuable consideration for what he had received; we can no more pretend to give a recompense to God than we can to merit any favour from him; but he desired to render something acceptable, something that God would be pleased with as the acknowledgment of a grateful mind. He asks God, <hi type="italic">What shall I render?</hi> Asks the priest, asks his friends, or rather asks himself, and communes with his own heart about it. Note, Having received many benefits from God, we are concerned to enquire, <hi type="italic">What shall we render?</hi> <div eID="gen12599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12600" type="x-p"/> 2. He resolves what returns he will make. <div eID="gen12600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12601" type="x-p"/> (1.) He will in the most devout and solemn manner offer up his praises and prayers to God, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.13">v. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.17">17</reference>. [1.] "<hi type="italic">I will take the cup of salvation,</hi> that is, I will offer the drink-offerings appointed by the law, in token of my thankfulness to God, and rejoice with my friends in God's goodness to me;" this is called <hi type="italic">the cup of deliverance</hi> because drunk in memory of his deliverance. The pious Jews had sometimes a <hi type="italic">cup of blessing,</hi> at their private meals, which the master of the family drank first of, with thanksgiving to God, and all at his table drank with him. But some understand it not of the cup that he would present to God, but of the cup that God would put into his hand. <hi type="italic">I will receive, First,</hi> The <hi type="italic">cup of affliction.</hi> Many good interpreters understand it of that cup, that bitter cup, which is yet sanctified to the saints, so that to them it is a cup of salvation. <reference osisRef="Phil.1.19">Phil. i. 19</reference>, <hi type="italic">This shall turn to my salvation;</hi> it is a means of spiritual health. David's sufferings were typical of Christ's, and we, in ours, have communion with his, and his cup was indeed a cup of salvation. "God, having bestowed so many benefits upon me, whatever cup he shall put into my hands I will readily take it, and not dispute it; welcome his holy will." Herein David spoke the language of the Son of David. <reference osisRef="John.18.11">John xviii. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">The cup that my Father has given me, shall I not</hi> take it and <hi type="italic">drink it? Secondly,</hi> The cup of consolation: "I will receive the benefits God bestows upon me as from his hand, and taste his love in them, as that which is <hi type="italic">the portion</hi> not only <hi type="italic">of my inheritance</hi> in the other world, but <hi type="italic">of my cup</hi> in this." [2.] <hi type="italic">I will offer to thee the sacrifice of thanksgiving,</hi> the thank-offerings which God required, <reference osisRef="Lev.7.11-Lev.7.12">Lev. vii. 11, 12</reference>, &c. Note, Those whose hearts are truly thankful will express their gratitude in thank-offerings. We must first <hi type="italic">give our ownselves</hi> to God as <hi type="italic">living sacrifices</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.1-Rom.12.2">Rom. xii. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Col.8.5">2 Cor. viii. 5</reference>), and then lay out of what we have for his honour in works of piety and charity. <hi type="italic">Doing good</hi> and <hi type="italic">communicating</hi> are <hi type="italic">sacrifices</hi> with which <hi type="italic">God is well pleased</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.15-Heb.13.16">Heb. xiii. 15, 16</reference>) and this must accompany our <hi type="italic">giving thanks to his name.</hi> If God has been bountiful to us, the least we can do in return is to be bountiful to the poor, <reference osisRef="Ps.16.2-Ps.16.3">Ps. xvi. 2, 3</reference>. Why should we offer that to God which costs us nothing? [3.] <hi type="italic">I will call upon the name of the Lord.</hi> This he had promised (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.2">v. 2</reference>) and here he repeats it, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.13">v. 13</reference> and again <reference osisRef="Ps.116.17">v. 17</reference>. If we have received kindness from a man like ourselves, we tell him that we hope we shall never trouble him again; but God is pleased to reckon the prayers of his people an honour to him, and a delight, and no trouble; and therefore, in gratitude for former mercies, we must seek to him for further mercies, and continue to <hi type="italic">call upon him.</hi> <div eID="gen12601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12602" type="x-p"/> (2.) He will always entertain good thoughts of God, as very tender of the lives and comforts of his people (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints,</hi> so precious that he will not gratify Saul, nor Absalom, nor any of David's enemies, with his death, how earnestly soever they desire it. This truth David had comforted himself with in the depth of his distress and danger; and, the event having confirmed it, he comforts others with it who might be in like manner exposed. God has a people, even in this world, that are his saints, his merciful ones, or men of mercy, that have received mercy from him and show mercy for his sake. The saints of God are mortal and dying; nay, there are those that desire their death, and labour all they can to hasten it, and sometimes prevail to be the death of them; but it is <hi type="italic">precious in the sight of the Lord; their life</hi> is so (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.1.13">2 Kings i. 13</reference>); their <hi type="italic">blood</hi> is so, <reference osisRef="Ps.72.14">Ps. lxxii. 14</reference>. God often wonderfully prevents the death of his saints when there is but a step between them and it; he takes special care about their death, to order it for the best in all the circumstances of it; and whoever kills them, how light soever they may make of it, they shall be made to pay dearly for it when inquisition is made for the blood of the saints, <reference osisRef="Matt.23.35">Matt. xxiii. 35</reference>. Though <hi type="italic">no man lays it to heart</hi> when <hi type="italic">the righteous perish,</hi> God will make it to appear that he lays it to heart. This should make us willing to die, to die for Christ, if we are called to it, that our death shall be registered in heaven; and let that be precious to us which is so to God. <div eID="gen12602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12603" type="x-p"/> (3.) He will oblige himself to be God's servant all his days. Having asked, <hi type="italic">What shall I render?</hi> here he surrenders himself, which was <hi type="italic">more than all burnt-offerings and sacrifice</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.16">v. 16</reference>): <hi type="italic">O Lord! truly I am thy servant.</hi> Here is, [1.] The relation in which David professes to stand to God: "<hi type="italic">I am thy servant;</hi> I choose to be so; I resolve to be so; I will live and die in thy service." He had called God's people, who are dear to him, <hi type="italic">his saints;</hi> but, when he comes to apply it to himself, he does not say, <hi type="italic">Truly I am thy saint</hi> (that looked too high a title for himself), but, <hi type="italic">I am thy servant.</hi> David was a king, and yet he glories in this, that he was God's servant. It is no disparagement, but an honour, to the greatest kings on earth, to be the servants of the God of heaven. David does not here compliment God, as it is common among men to say, <hi type="italic">I am your servant, Sir.</hi> No; "Lord, I am <hi type="italic">truly thy servant; thou knowest all things, thou knowest that I am so.</hi>" And he repeats it, as that which he took pleasure in the thoughts of and which he was resolved to abide by: "<hi type="italic">I am thy servant, I am thy servant.</hi> Let others serve what master they will, <hi type="italic">truly I am</hi> they <hi type="italic">servant.</hi>" [2.] The ground of that relation. Two ways men came to be servants:—<hi type="italic">First,</hi> by birth. "Lord, I was born in thy house; I am <hi type="italic">the son of thy handmaid,</hi> and therefore thine." It, is a great mercy to be the children of godly parents, as it obliges us to duty and is pleadable with God for mercy. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> By redemption. He that procured the release of a captive took him for his servant. "<hi type="italic">Lord, thou hast loosed my bonds;</hi> those sorrows of death that compassed me, thou hast discharged me from them, and therefore <hi type="italic">I am thy servant,</hi> and entitled to thy protection as well as obliged to thy work." <hi type="italic">The very bonds which thou hast loosed shall tie me faster unto thee.</hi> Patrick. <div eID="gen12603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12604" type="x-p"/> (4.) He will make conscience of paying his vows and making good what he had promised, not only that he would offer the sacrifices of praise, which he had vowed to bring, but perform all his other engagements to God, which he had laid himself under in the day of his affliction (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will pay my vows;</hi> and again, (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.18">v. 18</reference>), <hi type="italic">now in the presence of all his people.</hi> Note, Vows are debts that must be paid, for it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. He will pay his vows, [1.] Presently; he will not, like sorry debtors, delay the payment of them, or beg a day; but, "<hi type="italic">I will pay them now,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.4">Eccl. v. 4</reference>. [2.] Publicly; he will not huddle up his praises in a corner, but what service he has to do for God he will do it <hi type="italic">in the presence of all his people;</hi> nor for ostentation, but to show that he was not ashamed of the service of God, and that others might be invited to join with him. He will pay his vows in the courts of the tabernacle, where there was a crowd of Israelites attending, <hi type="italic">in the midst of Jerusalem,</hi> that he might bring devotion into more reputation.  <chapter eID="Ps.116"/> <div eID="gen12604" type="x-p"/>

entries.9f9fec2be7ad045ee5d00deea07b17350df84add: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6843"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 116</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.116.1-Ps.116.19">Psa 116:1-19</reference>. The writer celebrates the deliverance from extreme perils by which he was favored, and pledges grateful and pious public acknowledgments.</title> <div sID="gen10503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6843"/>1-2. A truly grateful love will be evinced by acts of worship, which calling on God expresses (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.13">Psa 116:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.16">Psa 55:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.86.7">86:7</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Ps.17.6">Psa 17:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.31.2">31:2</reference>). <div eID="gen10503" type="x-p"/>
entries.8bfc480eee55ace2d7c2e35e2c230eea54a2389b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6844"/><div sID="gen10504" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6844"/>3-4. For similar figures for distress see <reference osisRef="Ps.18.4">Psa 18:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.5">5</reference>.<div eID="gen10504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10505" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">gat hold upon me--</hi>Another sense ("found") of the same word follows, as we speak of disease finding us, and of our finding or catching disease. <div eID="gen10505" type="x-p"/>
entries.49c7942c881ba500eb2df8090efccd9a758efeb0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6845"/><div sID="gen10506" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6845"/>5-8. The relief which he asked is the result not of his merit, but of God's known pity and tenderness, which is acknowledged in assuring himself (his "soul," <reference osisRef="Ps.11.1">Psa 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">16:10</reference>) of rest and peace. All calamities [Psa 116:8] are represented by death, tears, and falling of the feet (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.13">Psa 56:13</reference>). <div eID="gen10506" type="x-p"/>
entries.d158be9bdf07c0c7e7335ea3cd003824637f7e54: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6846"/><div sID="gen10507" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6846"/><hi type="bold">9. walk before the Lord--</hi>act, or live under His favor and guidance (<reference osisRef="Gen.17.1">Ge 17:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.61.7">Psa 61:7</reference>).<div eID="gen10507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">land of the living--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Psa 27:13</reference>). <div eID="gen10508" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d458d677a121cfcc88173481f8dfacd7cc2597d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6847"/><div sID="gen10509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6847"/>10-11. Confidence in God opposed to distrust of men, as not reliable (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.8">Psa 68:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.9">9</reference>). He speaks from an experience of the result of his faith. <div eID="gen10509" type="x-p"/>
entries.80425f31aa1c05a983f9d9296db27bbcd90a88aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6849"/><div sID="gen10511" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6849"/>12-14. These are modes of expressing acts of worship (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.116.4">Psa 116:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.50.14">Psa 50:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.9">Jon 2:9</reference>). <div eID="gen10511" type="x-p"/>
entries.bbcb6134db9d7c68b5540a893e9edcd9288da975: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6852"/><div sID="gen10514" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6852"/>15-16. By the plea of being a homeborn servant, he intimates his claim on God's covenant love to His people. <div eID="gen10514" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9f42557a86eac2ce7c8dc49a919e31c4e4c12bc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6853"/><div sID="gen10515" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6853"/>17-19. An ampler declaration of his purpose, designating the place, the Lord's house, or earthly residence in Jerusalem. <chapter eID="Ps.116"/>

entries.dd68bcb3b1879b0fad4ea3faa1afe7aa9e7a924b: <div eID="gen22592" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22593" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22594" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22594" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22593" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22595" type="x-p"/> The psalmist praises God for his deliverance from thraldom, which he compares to death and the grave, <reference osisRef="Psa.116.1-Psa.116.9">Psa 116:1-9</reference>. The exercises through which he had passed, <reference osisRef="Psa.116.10">Psa 116:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.116.11">Psa 116:11</reference>. His gratitude for these mercies, and resolution to live to God's glory, <reference osisRef="Psa.116.12-Psa.116.19">Psa 116:12-19</reference>. <div eID="gen22595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22596" type="x-p"/> This Psalm is also without a title, and its author is unknown. It appears to have been written after the captivity, and to be a thanksgiving to God for that glorious event. The psalmist compares this captivity to death and the grave; and shows the happy return to the promised land, called here The land of the living. The people recollect the vows of God which were upon them, and purpose to fulfill them. They exhult at being enabled to worship God in the temple at Jerusalem. <div eID="gen22596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22597" type="x-p"/> The Syriac, which abounds in conjectural prefaces, supposes this Psalm to have been written on the occasion of Saul coming to the mouth of the cave in which David lay hidden; but spiritually taken, it relates to the bringing of a new people, the Gentiles, to the Christian faith. In a few MSS. this Psalm is joined to the preceding. Many think it relates wholly to the passion, death, and triumph of Christ. Most of the fathers were of this opinion. <div eID="gen22597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22598" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen22598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22599" type="x-p"/> I love the Lord because he hath heard - How vain and foolish is the talk, "To love God for his benefits to us is mercenary, and cannot be pure love!" Whether pure or impure, there is no other love that can flow from the heart of the creature to its Creator. We love him, said the holiest of Christ's disciples, because he first loved us; and the increase of our love and filial obedience is in proportion to the increased sense we have of our obligation to him. We love him for the benefits bestowed on us. Love begets love.
entries.0c335bba400f87aea811a3bac661ac1c8cf56fec: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen22599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22600" type="x-p"/> Because he hath inclined his ear - The psalmist represents himself to be so sick and weak, that he could scarcely speak. The Lord, in condescension to this weakness, is here considered as bowing down his ear to the mouth of the feeble suppliant, that he may receive every word of his prayer. <div eID="gen22600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22601" type="x-p"/> Therefore will I call upon him - I have had such blessed success in my application to him, that I purpose to invoke him as long as I shall live. He that prays much will be emboldened to pray more, because none can supplicate the throne of grace in vain.
entries.e4780e4d5cd78a4983a3571cbd94e64aee8a0ac6: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen22601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22602" type="x-p"/> The sorrows of death - חבלי מות chebley maveth, the cables or cords of death; alluding to their bonds and fetters during their captivity; or to the cords by which a criminal is bound who is about to be led out to execution; or to the bandages in which the dead were enveloped, when head, arms, body, and limbs were all laced down together. <div eID="gen22602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22603" type="x-p"/> The pains of hell - מצרי שאול metsarey sheol the straitnesses of the grave. So little expectation was there of life, that he speaks as if he were condemned, executed, and closed up in the tomb. Or, he may refer here to the small niches in cemeteries, where the coffins of the dead were placed. <div eID="gen22603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22604" type="x-p"/> Because this Psalm has been used in the thanksgiving of women after safe delivery, it has been supposed that the pain suffered in the act of parturition was equal for the time to the torments of the damned. But this supposition is shockingly absurd; the utmost power of human nature could not, for a moment, endure the wrath of God, the deathless worm, and the unquenchable fire. The body must die, be decomposed, and be built up on indestructible principles, before this punishment can be borne.
entries.0847d82ba38402195e650414f6f19ced87a50194: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen22604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22605" type="x-p"/> Gracious is the Lord - In his own nature. <div eID="gen22605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22606" type="x-p"/> And righteous - In all his dealings with men. <div eID="gen22606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22607" type="x-p"/> Our God is merciful - Of tender compassion to all penitents.
entries.41996d98036dc5756e2e18bac34c49de62176ced: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen22607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22608" type="x-p"/> The Lord preserved the simple - פתאים pethaim, which all the Versions render little ones. Those who are meek and lowly of heart, who feel the spirit of little children, these he preserves, as he does little children; and he mentions this circumstance, because the Lord has a peculiar regard for these young ones, and gives his angels charge concerning them. Were it otherwise, children are exposed to so many dangers and deaths, that most of them would fall victims to accidents in their infancy.
entries.50f8bd1c545eb3d37587c0f048cd339ee38c139f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen22608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22609" type="x-p"/> Return unto thy rest, O my soul - God is the center to which all immortal spirits tend, and in connection with which alone they can find rest. Every thing separated from its center is in a state of violence; and, if intelligent, cannot be happy. All human souls, while separated from God by sin, are in a state of violence, agitation, and misery. From God all spirits come; to him all must return, in order to be finally happy. This is true in the general case; though, probably, the rest spoken of here means the promised land, into which they were now returning. <div eID="gen22609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22610" type="x-p"/> A proof of the late origin of this Psalm is exhibited in this verse, in the words למנוחיכי limenuchaichi, "to thy rest," and עליכי alaichi, "to thee," which are both Chaldaisms.
entries.1f924dd6b67af6432baaeafc61f38c3d47138ad1: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen22610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22611" type="x-p"/> Thou hast delivered my soul from death - Thou hast rescued my life from the destruction to which it was exposed. <div eID="gen22611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22612" type="x-p"/> Mine eyes from tears - Thou hast turned my sorrow into joy. <div eID="gen22612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22613" type="x-p"/> My feet from falling - Thou hast taken me out of the land of snares and pitfalls, and brought me into a plain path. How very near does our ancient mother tongue come to this: For thou he nerode sawle mine of deathe, eapan mine of tearum; fet mine of slide. And this language is but a little improved in the old Psalter: - <div eID="gen22613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22614" type="x-p"/> For he toke my saule fra dede; my eghen fra teres; my fete fra slippyng.
entries.9f9dc95354799ed3d609ea9ba2178a32e90b35ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen22614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22615" type="x-p"/> I will walk before the Lord - אתהלך ethhallech, I will set myself to walk. I am determined to walk; my eyes are now bright ened, so that I can see; my feet are strengthened, so that I can walk; and my soul is alive, so that I can walk with the living. <div eID="gen22615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22616" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate, the Septuagint, the Ethiopic, the Arabic, and the Anglo-Saxon end this Psalm here, which is numbered the cxivth; and begin with the tenth verse another Psalm, which they number cxvth; but this division is not acknowledged by the Hebrew, Chaldee, and Syriac.
entries.11539ca42afd59c34e875ba32cc0cd890631d493: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen22616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22617" type="x-p"/> I believed, therefere have I spoken - Distressed and afflicted as I was, I ever believed thy promises to be true; but I had great struggles to maintain my confidence; for my afflictions were great, oppressive, and of long standing. <div eID="gen22617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22618" type="x-p"/> It is scarcely worth observing that the letters called heemantic by the Hebrew grammarians, and which are used in forming the derivatives from the roots, are taken from the first word in this verse, האמנתי heemanti, "I have believed;" as the prefixes in that language are found in the technical words משה וכלב Mosheh vecaleb, "Moses and Caleb;" and the formatives of the future are found in the word איתן eythan, "strength."
entries.9ef96f12b7fa87bd3c4d1509293f0472e8dbaf60: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen22618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22619" type="x-p"/> I said in my haste - This is variously translated: I said in my Light, Chaldee. In my excess, or ecstasy, Vulgate. In my ecstasy, εκστασει, Septuagint. fi tahayury, in my giddiness, Arabic. In my fear or tremor, Syriac. I quoth in outgoing mine, when I was beside myself, Anglo-Saxon. In myn oute passyng, old Psalter. When passion got the better of my reason, when I looked not at God, but at my afflictions, and the impossibility of human relief. <div eID="gen22619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22620" type="x-p"/> All men are liars - כל האדם כזב col haadam cozeb, "the whole of man is a lie." Falsity is diffused through his nature; deception proceeds from his tongue; his actions are often counterfeit. He is imposed on by others, and imposes in his turn; and on none is there any dependence till God converts their heart. "O what a thing were man, if his attires <div eID="gen22620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22621" type="x-p"/> Should alter with his mind, <div eID="gen22621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22622" type="x-p"/> And, like a dolphin's skin, <div eID="gen22622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22623" type="x-p"/> His clothes combine with his desires! <div eID="gen22623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22624" type="x-p"/> Surely if each one saw another's heart, <div eID="gen22624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22625" type="x-p"/> There would be no commerce; <div eID="gen22625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22626" type="x-p"/> All would disperse, And live apart." <div eID="gen22626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22627" type="x-p"/> Hebert. <div eID="gen22627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22628" type="x-p"/> To the same purpose I shall give the following Italian proverb: - <div eID="gen22628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22629" type="x-p"/> Con arte e con inganno, <div eID="gen22629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22630" type="x-p"/> Si vive mezzo l'anno. <div eID="gen22630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22631" type="x-p"/> Con inganno e con arte <div eID="gen22631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22632" type="x-p"/> Si vive l' altro parti. "Men live half the year by deceit and by art; <div eID="gen22632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22633" type="x-p"/> By art and deceit men live the other part." <div eID="gen22633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22634" type="x-p"/> Who gives this bad character of mankind? Man.
entries.ebd79ac2272309d0fb49650b5652d31dbe41de7b: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen22634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22635" type="x-p"/> What shall I render - מה אשיב mah ashib, "What shall I return?" <div eID="gen22635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22636" type="x-p"/> For his benefits - תגמולוהי tagmulohi, "His retributions," the returns he had made to my prayers and faith.
entries.b93789509547a11d315b8026844e2298f417736b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen22636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22637" type="x-p"/> I will take the cup of salvation - Literally, The cup of salvation, or deliverance, will I lift up. Alluding to the action in taking the cup of blessing among the Jews, which, when the person or master of the family lifted up, he said these words, "Blessed be the Lord, the Maker of the world, who has created the fruit of the vine!" <div eID="gen22637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22638" type="x-p"/> But it may probably allude to the libation-offering, <reference osisRef="Num.28.7">Num 28:7</reference>; for the three last verses seem to intimate that the psalmist was now at the temple, offering the meat-offering, drink-offering, and sacrifices to the Lord. Cup is often used by the Hebrews to denote plenty or abundance. So, the cup of trembling, an abundance of misery; the cup of salvation, an abundance of happiness. <div eID="gen22638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22639" type="x-p"/> And call upon the name of the Lord - I will invoke his name, that I may get more of the same blessings; for the only return that God requires is, that we ask for more. Who is like God? One reason why we should never more come to a fellow-mortal for a favor is, we have received so many already. A strong reason why we should claim the utmost salvation of God is, because we are already so much in debt to his mercy. Now this is the only way we have of discharging our debts to God; and yet, strange to tell, every such attempt to discharge the debt only serves to increase it! Yet, notwithstanding, the debtor and creditor are represented as both pleased, both profited, and both happy in each other! Reader, pray to him, invoke his name; receive the cup - accept the abundance of salvation which he has provided thee, that thou mayest love and serve him with a perfect heart.
entries.1dca5dd03372c771c471dd76113eff6ac867e907: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen22639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22640" type="x-p"/> I will pay my vows unto the Lord now in the presence of all his people - He was probably now bringing his offering to the temple. These words are repeated, <reference osisRef="Psa.116.18">Psa 116:18</reference>.
entries.c03571d13b0002690d19545db1b30c76454f589c: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen22640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22641" type="x-p"/> Precious in the sight of the Lord - Many have understood this verse as meaning, "the saints are too precious in the Lord's sight, lightly to give them over to death:" and this, Calmet contends, is the true sense of the text. Though they have many enemies, their lives are precious in his sight, and their foes shall not prevail against them.
entries.862b43025b775b43309ecce566a68546c19c448b: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen22641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22642" type="x-p"/> I am thy servant - Thou hast preserved me alive. I live with, for, and to Thee. I am thy willing domestic, the son of thine handmaid - like one born in thy house of a woman already thy property. I am a servant, son of thy servant, made free by thy kindness; but, refusing to go out, I have had my ear bored to thy door-post, and am to continue by free choice in thy house for ever. He alludes here to the case of the servant who, in the year of jubilee being entitled to his liberty, refused to leave his master's house; and suffered his ear to be bored to the door-post, as a proof that by his own consent he agreed to continue in his master's house for ever.
entries.f999eca200e747ec5426b7ea3b63f1901feb1076: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen22642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22643" type="x-p"/> I will offer to thee - As it is most probable that this Psalm celebrates the deliverance from Babylon, it is no wonder that we find the psalmist so intent on performing the rites of his religion in the temple at Jerusalem, which had been burnt with fire, and was now reviving out of its ruins, the temple service having been wholly interrupted for nearly four-score years.
entries.c1cf51c356b4541353cd491fbdb27a63a00fc530: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen22643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22644" type="x-p"/> In the midst of thee, O Jerusalem - He speaks as if present in the city, offering his vowed sacrifices in the temple to the Lord. <div eID="gen22644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22645" type="x-p"/> Most of this Psalm has been applied to our Lord and his Church; and in this way it has been considered as prophetic; and, taken thus, it is innocently accommodated, and is very edifying. This is the interpretation given of the whole by the old Psalter.  <chapter eID="Ps.116"/> <div eID="gen22645" type="x-p"/>

entries.2f98738f929cadeccc219c76ead4651017ed831b: <div eID="gen10101" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Thanksgiving Song of One Who Has Escaped from Death</title> <div sID="gen10102" type="x-p"/> We have here another anonymous Psalm closing with <hi type="italic">Hallelujah</hi>. It is not a supplicatory song with a hopeful prospect before it like Ps 115, but a thanksgiving song with a fresh recollection of some deadly peril that has just been got the better of; and is not, like Ps 115, from the mouth of the church, but from the lips of an individual who distinguishes himself from the church. It is an individual that has been delivered who here praises the loving-kindness he has experienced in the language of the tenderest affection. The lxx has divided this deeply fervent song into two parts, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.1-Ps.116.9">Psa 116:1-9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.10-Ps.116.19">Psa 116:10-19</reference>, and made two Hallelujah-Psalms out of it; whereas it unites <reference osisRef="Ps.114.1-Ps.114.8">Psa 114:1-8</reference> and Ps 115 into one. The four sections or strophes, the beginnings of which correspond to one another (<reference osisRef="Ps.116.1">Psa 116:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.116.10">Psa 116:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.5">Psa 116:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.116.15">Psa 116:15</reference>), are distinctly separate. The words אקרא וּבשׁם ה are repeated three times. In the first instance they are retrospective, but then swell into an always more full-toned vow of thanksgiving. The late period of its composition makes itself known not only in the strong Aramaic colouring of the form of the language, which adopts all kinds of embellishments, but also in many passages borrowed from the pre-exilic Psalms. The very opening, and still more so the progress, of the first strophe reminds one of Ps 18, and becomes an important hint for the exposition of the Psalm.
entries.b5b3730d48c423daa14d9ca3c957c768c10b8a69: <reference osisRef="Ps.116.1-Ps.116.4">Psa 116:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen10102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10103" type="x-p"/> Not only is כּי אהבתּי “I love (like, am well pleased) that,” like ἀγαπῶ ὅτι, Thucydides vi. 36, contrary to the usage of the language, but the thought, “I love that Jahve answereth me,” is also tame and flat, and inappropriate to the continuation in Psa 116:2. Since <reference osisRef="Ps.116.3-Ps.116.4">Psa 116:3-4</reference> have come from <reference osisRef="Ps.18.5-Ps.18.17">Psa 18:5-17</reference>, אהבתּי is to be understood according to ארחמך in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.2">Psa 18:2</reference>, so that it has the following יהוה as its object, not it is true grammatically, but logically. The poet is fond of this pregnant use of the verb without an expressed object, cf. אקרא in <reference osisRef="Ps.116.2">Psa 116:2</reference>, and האמנתּי in Psa 116:10. The <hi type="italic">Pasek</hi> after ישׁמע is intended to guard against the blending of the final <hi type="italic">a‛</hi> with the initial <hi type="italic">'a</hi> of אדני (cf. Psa 56:1-13 :18; <reference osisRef="Ps.5.2">Psa 5:2</reference>, in Baer). In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.116.1">Psa 116:1</reference></hi> the accentuation prevents the rendering <hi type="italic">vocem orationis meae</hi> (Vulgate, lxx) by means of <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>. The <hi type="italic">ı̂</hi> of קולי will therefore no more be the archaic connecting vowel (Ew. §211, <hi type="italic">b</hi>) than in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.42">Lev 26:42</reference>; the poet has varied the genitival construction of <reference osisRef="Ps.28.6">Psa 28:6</reference> to the permutative. The second כי, following close upon the first, makes the continuation of the confirmation retrospective. “In my days” is, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.39.8">Isa 39:8</reference>, Bar. 4:20, cf. בחיּי in <reference osisRef="Ps.63.5">Psa 63:5</reference>, and frequently, equivalent to “so long as I live.” We even here hear the tone of Ps 18 (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.2">Psa 18:2</reference>), which is continued in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.3-Ps.18.4">Psa 18:3-4</reference> as a freely borrowed passage. Instead of the “bands” (of Hades) there, the expression here is מצרי, <hi type="italic">angustiae</hi>, plural of meetsar, after the form מסב in <reference osisRef="Ps.118.5">Psa 118:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.1.3">Lam 1:3</reference> (Böttcher, <hi type="italic">De inferis</hi>, §423); the straitnesses of Hades are deadly perils which can scarcely be escaped. The futures אמצא and אקרא, by virtue of the connection, refer to the contemporaneous past. אנּה (viz., בלישׁן בקשׁה, i.e., in a suppliant sense) is written with <hi type="italic">He</hi> instead of <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi> here and in five other instances, as the Masora observes. It has its fixed <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> in the first syllable, in accordance with which it is to be pronounced <hi type="italic">ānna</hi> (like בּתּים, <hi type="italic">bāttim</hi>), and has an accented <hi type="italic">ultima</hi> not merely on account of the following יהוה = אדני (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.3.8">Psa 3:8</reference>), but in every instance; for even where (the <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> having been changed into a conjunctive) it is supplied with two different accents, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.50.17">Gen 50:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.31">Exo 32:31</reference>, the second indicates the tone-syllable.<note placement="foot">Kimchi, mistaking the vocation of the <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi>, regards אנּה (אנּא) as <hi type="italic">Milel</hi>. But the Palestinian and the Babylonian systems of pointing coincide in this, that the beseeching אנא (אנה) is <hi type="italic">Milra</hi>, and the interrogatory אנה <hi type="italic">Milel</hi> (with only two exceptions in our text, which is fixed according to the Palestinian Masora, viz., <reference osisRef="Ps.139.7">Psa 139:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.1.28">Deu 1:28</reference>, where the following word begins with <hi type="italic">Aleph</hi>), and these modes of accenting accord with the origin of the two particles. Pinsker (<hi type="italic">Einleitung</hi>, S. xiii.) insinuates against the Palestinian system, that in the cases where אנא has two accents the pointing was not certain of the correct accentuation, only from a deficient knowledge of the bearings of the case.</note> <div eID="gen10103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10104" type="x-p"/> Instead now of repeating “and Jahve answered me,” the poet indulges in a laudatory confession of general truths which have been brought vividly to his mind by the answering of his prayer that he has experienced.
entries.a947b42237979b1491d0134cdb6c61b943a9cbae: <reference osisRef="Ps.116.5-Ps.116.9">Psa 116:5-9</reference> <div eID="gen10104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10105" type="x-p"/> With “gracious” and “compassionate” is here associated, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.112.4">Psa 112:4</reference>, the term “righteous,” which comprehends within itself everything that Jahve asserts concerning Himself in Exo 34:6. from the words “and abundant in goodness and truth” onwards. His love is turned especially toward the simple (lxx τὰ νήπια, cf. <reference osisRef="Matt.11.25">Mat 11:25</reference>), who stand in need of His protection and give themselves over to it. פּתאים, as in <reference osisRef="Prov.9.6">Pro 9:6</reference>, is a mode of writing blended out of פּתאים and פּתיים. The poet also has experienced this love in a time of impotent need. דּלּותי is accented on the <hi type="italic">ultima</hi> here, and not as in <reference osisRef="Ps.142.7">Psa 142:7</reference> on the <hi type="italic">penult</hi>. The accentuation is regulated by some phonetic or rhythmical law that has not yet been made clear (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.19.17">Job 19:17</reference>).<note placement="foot">The national grammarians, so far as we are acquainted with them, furnish no explanation. De Balmis believes that these <hi type="italic">Milra</hi> forms דּלּותי, בּלּותי, and the like, must be regarded as infinitives, but at the same time confirms the difference of views existing on this point.</note> יהושׁיע is a resolved <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> form, the use of which became common in the later period of the language, but is not alien to the earlier period, especially in poetry (Ps 45:18, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.81.6">Psa 81:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.47">1Sa 17:47</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.5">Isa 52:5</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Ps.116.7">Psa 116:7</reference> we hear the form of soliloquy which has become familiar to us from <reference osisRef="Ps.42.1">Psa 42:1</reference>; Ps 103. שׁוּבי is <hi type="italic">Milra</hi> here, as also in two other instances. The plural מנוּחים signifies full, complete rest, as it is found only in God; and the suffix in the address to the soul is <hi type="italic">ajchi</hi> for <hi type="italic">ajich</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.103.3">Psa 103:3</reference>-5. The perfect גּמל states that which is a matter of actual experience, and is corroborated in <reference osisRef="Ps.116.8">Psa 116:8</reference> in retrospective perfects. In <reference osisRef="Ps.116.8-Ps.116.9">Psa 116:8-9</reference> we hear Ps 56:14 again amplified; and if we add <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Psa 27:13</reference>, then we see as it were to the bottom of the origin of the poet’s thoughts. מן־דּמעה belongs still more decidedly than יהושׁיע to the resolved forms which multiply in the later period of the language. In <reference osisRef="Ps.116.9">Psa 116:9</reference> the poet declares the result of the divine deliverance. The <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. אתהלּך denotes a free and contented going to and fro; and instead of “the land of the living,” <reference osisRef="Ps.27.13">Psa 27:13</reference>, the expression here is “the lands (ארצות), i.e., the broad land, of the living.” There he walks forth, with nothing to hinder his feet or limit his view, in the presence of Jahve, i.e., having his Deliverer from death ever before his eyes.
entries.a27bb7039107f380a9d2ca9ebf699fd759824ed3: <reference osisRef="Ps.116.10-Ps.116.14">Psa 116:10-14</reference> <div eID="gen10105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10106" type="x-p"/> Since כּי אדבּר does not introduce anything that could become an object of belief, האמין is absolute here: to have faith, just as in <reference osisRef="Job.24.22">Job 24:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.24">Job 29:24</reference>, with לא it signifies “to be without faith, i.e., to despair.” But how does it now proceed? The lxx renders ἐπίστευσα, διὸ ἐλάλησα, which the apostle makes use of in <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.13">2Co 4:13</reference>, without our being therefore obliged with Luther to render<hi type="italic">: I believe, therefore I speak</hi>; כי does not signify διὸ. Nevertheless כי might according to the sense be used for לכן, if it had to be rendered with Hengstenberg: “I believed, therefore I spake,hy but I was very much plagued.” But this assertion does not suit this connection, and has, moreover, no support in the syntax. It might more readily be rendered: “I have believed that I should yet speak, i.e., that I should once more have a deliverance of God to celebrate;” but the connection of the parallel members, which is then only lax, is opposed to this. Hitzig’s attempted interpretation, “I trust, when (כּי as in <reference osisRef="Jer.12.1">Jer 12:1</reference>) I should speak: I am greatly afflicted,” i.e., “I have henceforth confidence, so that I shall not suffer myself to be drawn away into the expression of despondency,” does not commend itself, since <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.116.10">Psa 116:10</reference></hi> is a complaining, but not therefore as yet a desponding assertion of the reality. Assuming that האמנתּי and אמרתּי in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.116.11">Psa 116:11</reference></hi> stand on the same line in point of time, it seems that it must be interpreted <hi type="italic">I had faith, for I spake</hi> (was obliged to speak); but אדבר, separated from האמנתי by כי, is opposed to the colouring relating to the contemporaneous past. Thus <reference osisRef="Ps.116.10">Psa 116:10</reference> will consequently contain the issue of that which has been hitherto experienced: <hi type="italic">I</hi> have gathered up faith and <hi type="italic">believe</hi> henceforth, <hi type="italic">when I speak</hi> (have to speak, must speak): <hi type="italic">I am deeply afflicted</hi> (ענה as in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.67">Psa 119:67</reference>, cf. Arab. <hi type="italic">‛nâ</hi>, to be bowed down, more particularly in captivity, whence Arab. <hi type="italic">'l - ‛nât</hi>, those who are bowed down). On the other hand, <reference osisRef="Ps.116.11">Psa 116:11</reference> is manifestly a retrospect. He believes now, for he is thoroughly weaned from putting trust in men: <hi type="italic">I said in my despair</hi> (taken from <reference osisRef="Ps.31.23">Psa 31:23</reference>), the result of my deeply bowed down condition: <hi type="italic">All men are liars</hi> (πᾶς ἄνθρωπος ψεύστης, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.4">Rom 3:4</reference>). Forsaken by all the men from whom he expected succour and help, he experienced the truth and faithfulness of God. Striding away over this thought, he asks in <reference osisRef="Ps.116.12">Psa 116:12</reference> how he is to give thanks to God for all His benefits. מה is an adverbial accusative for בּמּה, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.44.16">Gen 44:16</reference>, and the substantive תּגּמוּל, in itself a later formation, has besides the Chaldaic plural suffix <hi type="italic">ôhi</hi>, which is without example elsewhere in Hebrew. The poet says in <reference osisRef="Ps.116.13">Psa 116:13</reference> how alone he can and will give thanks to his Deliverer, by using a figure taken from the Passover (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.27">Mat 26:27</reference>), the memorial repast in celebration of the redemption out of Egypt. The cup of salvation is that which is raised aloft and drunk amidst thanksgiving for the manifold and abundant salvation (ישׁוּעות) experienced. קרא בשׁם ה is the usual expression for a solemn and public calling upon and proclamation of the Name of God. In <reference osisRef="Ps.116.14">Psa 116:14</reference> this thanksgiving is more minutely designated as שׁלמי נדר, which the poet now discharges. A common and joyous eating and drinking in the presence of God was associated with the <hi type="italic">shelamim</hi>. נא (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.115.2">Psa 115:2</reference>) in the freest application gives a more animated tone to the word with which it stands. Because he is impelled frankly and freely to give thanks before the whole congregation, נא stands beside נגד, and נגד, moreover, has the intentional <hi type="italic">ah</hi>.
entries.e4c0fe8ee0125bb5b67aa84479abe36f2353e31d: <reference osisRef="Ps.116.15-Ps.116.19">Psa 116:15-19</reference> <div eID="gen10106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10107" type="x-p"/> From what he has experienced the poet infers that the saints of Jahve are under His most especial providence. Instead of המּות the poet, who is fond of such embellishments, chooses the pathetic form המּותה, and consequently, instead of the genitival construct state (מות), the construction with the <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> of “belonging to.” It ought properly to be “soul” or “blood,” as in the primary passage Psa 72:14. But the observation of Grotius: <hi type="italic">quae pretiosa sunt, non facile largimur</hi>, applies also to the expression “death.” The death of His saints is no trifling matter with God; He does not lightly suffer it to come about; He does not suffer His own to be torn away from Him by death.<note placement="foot">The Apostolic Constitutions (vi. 30) commend the singing of these and other words of the Psalms at the funerals of those who have departed in the faith (cf. Augusti, <hi type="italic">Denkwürdigkeiten</hi>, ix. 563). In the reign of the Emperor Decius, Babylas Bishop of Antioch, full of blessed hope, met death singing these words.</note> <div eID="gen10107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10108" type="x-p"/> After this the poet goes on beseechingly: <hi type="italic">ānnáh Adonaj</hi>. The prayer itself is not contained in פּתּחתּ למוסרי - for he is already rescued, and the perfect as a precative is limited to such utterances spoken in the tone of an exclamation as we find in <reference osisRef="Job.21.16">Job 21:16</reference> - but remains unexpressed; it lies wrapped up as it were in this heartfelt <hi type="italic">ānnáh</hi>: Oh remain still so gracious to me as Thou hast already proved Thyself to me. The poet rejoices in and is proud of the fact that he may call himself the servant of God. With אמתך he is mindful of his pious mother (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.86.16">Psa 86:16</reference>). The Hebrew does not form a feminine, עבדּה; Arab. <hi type="italic">amata</hi> signifies a maid, who is not, as such, also Arab. <hi type="italic">‛abdat</hi>, a slave. The dative of the object, למוסרי (from מוסרים for the more usual מוסרות), is used with פתחת instead of the accusative after the Aramaic manner, but it does also occur in the older Hebrew (e.g., <reference osisRef="Job.19.3">Job 19:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">Isa 53:11</reference>). The purpose of publicly giving thanks to the Gracious One is now more full-toned here at the close. Since such emphasis is laid on the Temple and the congregation, what is meant is literal thank-offerings in payment of vows. In בּתוככי (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.135.9">Psa 135:9</reference>) we have in the suffix the ancient and Aramaic <hi type="italic">i</hi> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.116.7">Psa 116:7</reference>) for the third time. With אנּה the poet clings to Jahve, with נגדּה־נּא to the congregation, and with בּתוככי to the holy city. The one thought that fills his whole soul, and in which the song which breathes forth his soul dies away, is <hi type="italic">Hallelujah</hi>.  <chapter eID="Ps.116"/> <div eID="gen10108" type="x-p"/>

entries.3b55d64c3d4764710c11f83e35fb80d5017b903f:
PSALM 116
David, being delivered out of very great dangers, relates what cruel torment and anguish of mind he endured, and then how remarkably he was preserved by God. The desperate state of matters with him tended to make the power of God in his preservation more conspicuous; for had not God interposed for his deliverance, all hope would have failed. In this way he stirs himself up to gratitude, and acknowledges that he can make no other return to him for his innumerable benefits.
This psalm is without a title in the Hebrew, although the LXX. Have prefixed to it Hallelujah, with which Psalm 115 ends. There have been various conjectures among interpreters as to its author. Some ascribe it to Hezekiah, and suppose it to relate to his recovery from the dangerous sickness recorded in Isaiah 38. Others think that it was composed by David upon his deliverance from the rebellion excited by his son Absalom, after which he immediately had liberty to return to the sanctuary and public assembly at Jerusalem, verses 14, 18, and 19. This opinion is confirmed from verse 11, in which he speaks of having for a time, under the sad experience of human treachery and deception, pronounced all men to be liars; a state of feeling more applicable to David’s distressed circumstances during the rebellion of his son, than to Hezekiah on his recovery from sickness.
Psalm 116:1-4
1. I have loved, because Jehovah shall hear the voice of my supplication. 2. Because he hath inclined his ear to me, and during my days I will call upon him. 3. The snares
The root of the Hebrew word חבלי, cheblei, here rendered snares, “is חבל, which signifies to bind, and in Piel conj., to pain, or torment. Geseius, in his Thesaurus, under חבל, says: — ‘Pi. i. q. Kal, No. 1, torsit, inde cum tormentis et doloribus enixa est ’ חבל consequently signifies pain, or cable. It would seem from the verb to which it is a subject, that the latter is the more suitable sense, whilst the parallelism is in favor of the former. The former, however, is here contained in the latter, for the expression חבלי מות alludes to the custom of binding the victims for slaughter, or malefactors when taken to the place of execution; which binding was productive of great pain.” — Phillips. See volume 1, page 264. Cresswell reads, “The straits of the grave, that is, the terrors of instant death, had found me.”
of death compassed me,
“ — ‘compassed me.’ The original word אפף expresses the repetition of the encircling of the toils. They surrounded him again and again.” — Horsley.
and the sorrows of the grave found me:
Fry’s translation of this clause is: —
“The nets of Hades had caught hold upon me;”
on which he has the following note: — “Or, according to the usual meaning of צור and צרר, ‘the pangs or pains of hell.’ It is not impossible, indeed, that it should be derived from נצר; we might then render, ‘The purveyors of Hades had found me:’ and the imagery, at any rate, seems to be taken from the toils of the hunter. Michaelis would read מצודי, ‘nets,’ instead of מצורי, pangs; but it is very probable that, without any change, מצורי signifies some part of the apparatus of hunting. ‘מצר a strait, distress, angustia ’ Psalm 118:5; 116:3; Lamentations 1:3. In which last text, Mr Lowth says that ‘there is a metaphor from those that hunt a prey, which they drive into some strait and narrow passage, from whence there is no making an escape.’”
I found tribulation and grief. 4. And I will call upon the name of Jehovah; I beseech thee, O Jehovah! deliver my soul.
 
1 I have loved, because Jehovah will hear the voice of my supplication. At the very commencement of this psalm David avows that he was attracted with the sweetness of God’s goodness, to place his hope and confidence in him alone. This abrupt mode of speaking, I have loved, is the more emphatic, intimating that he could receive joy and repose nowhere but in God. We know that our hearts will be always wandering after fruitless pleasures, and harassed with care, until God knit them to himself. This distemper David affirms was removed from him, because he felt that God was indeed propitious towards him. And, having found by experience that, in general, they who call upon God are happy, he declares that no allurements shall draw him away from God. When, therefore, he says, I have loved, it imports that, without God, nothing would be pleasant or agreeable to him. From this we are instructed that those who have been heard by God, but do not place themselves entirely under his guidance and guardianship, have derived little advantage from the experience of his grace.
The second verse also refers to the same subject, excepting that the latter clause admits of a very appropriate meaning, which expositors overlook. The phrase, during my days I will call upon him, is uniformly understood by them to mean, I, who hitherto have been so successful in addressing God, will pursue the same course all my life long. But it should be considered whether it may not be equally appropriate that the days of David be regarded as denoting a fit season of asking assistance, the season when he was hard pressed by necessity. I am not prevented from adopting this signification, because it may be said that the prophet employs the future tense of the verb אקרא, ekra. In the first verse also, the term, he shall hear, is to be understood in the past tense, he has heard, in which case the copulative conjunction would require to be taken as an adverb of time, when, a circumstance this by no means unusual among the Hebrews. The scope of the passage will run very well thus: Because he has bowed his ear to me when I called upon him in the time of my adversity, and even at the season, too, when I was reduced to the greatest straits. If any are disposed to prefer the former exposition, I will not dispute the matter with them. The subsequent context, however, appears to countenance the latter meaning, in which David commences energetically to point out what those days were. And, with the design of magnifying God’s glory according to its desert, he says that there was no way of his escaping from death, for he was like one among enemies, bound with fetters and chains, from whom all hope of deliverance was cut off. He acknowledges, therefore, that he was subjected to death, that he was overtaken and seized, so that escape was impossible. And as he declares that he was bound by the cords of death, so he, at the same the adds, that he fell into tribulation and sorrow And here he confirms what he said formerly, that when he seemed to be most forsaken of God, that was truly the proper time, and the right season for him to give himself to prayer.
Psalm 116:5-9
5. Jehovah is gracious and just; our God is merciful. 6. Jehovah guards the simple; I was brought low, and he saved me. 7. Return, O my soul! into thy rest; for Jehovah hath recompensed unto thee. 8. Because thou hast delivered my soul from death, mine eyes from tears, and my feet from falling. 9. I will walk in the presence of Jehovah in the land of the living.

                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This Psalm contains a solemn thanksgiving to God for a glo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rious deliverance from grievous and dangerous calamities, as also from great perplexities and terrors of mind arising from the sence of Gods displeasure.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="1">1 I Love the LORD, because he hath heard my voice, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> my supplications.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Then called I upon the Name of the LORD: O LORD, I beseech thee, deliver my soul.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 Gracious is the LORD <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">This he mentions either, 1. as that which he found by experience in answer to his prayers: or, 2. as the argument by which he encouraged himself to pray.</ns0:note>, and righteous <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Therefore he will maintain me and my just cause against my unrighteous op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressors, and perform his promises, and save those who faith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fully serve him and put their trust in him.</ns0:note>: yea, our God <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> merciful.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 The LORD preserveth the simple <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Sincere and plain-hearted persons, who dare not use those frauds and crasty and wicked artifices in saving them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves or destroying their enemies, but wait upon God with honest hearts in his way and for his time of deliverance.
